items.answer: Globalisation
items.markingKey: Globalisation: the process by which the world’s economies, cultures and peoples are becoming more connected and interdependent. [1]

items.stem: Country T exported goods and services worth US$150 billion and imported goods and services worth US$90 billion in one year. Its GDP was US$600 billion. Explain what a high trade-to-GDP percentage suggests about the country.
items.answer: It is very open and interdependent with the global economy, so it benefits from trade but is vulnerable to changes in world demand and supply chains.
items.markingKey: 1 mark openness; 1 mark vulnerability [2]

items.stem: Country T exported goods and services worth US$200 billion and imported goods and services worth US$180 billion in one year. Its GDP was US$400 billion. (a) Calculate total trade (exports + imports) as a percentage of GDP. (b) Suggest two ways the country could increase its exports.
items.answer: (a) 95% (b) Join trade agreements to reduce tariffs; improve ports and transport; attract foreign companies; develop higher-value manufacturing or services.

items.stem: “Globalisation has brought more benefits than problems to the world.” How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Agree: World trade has grown hugely, creating jobs and lowering prices; hundreds of millions have escaped extreme poverty in countries such as China and India. Faster communication spreads knowledge and technology. Disagree: Benefits are unequal; some workers face low wages and poor conditions. Transport and production increase carbon emissions and pollution. Supply chains are vulnerable (Suez 2021, COVID-19). Local cultures and businesses may be lost. Judgement: Globalisation has brought large economic benefits, but they are unevenly shared and come with environmental costs.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: Explain two advantages and two disadvantages of TNCs for host countries.
items.answer: Advantages: jobs, training, investment in infrastructure, tax revenue and exports. Disadvantages: low wages and poor conditions, profits sent abroad, pollution, local firms out-competed, the TNC may leave if costs rise.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each point [4]

items.stem: A study of a T-shirt sold for US$25 in Europe estimated how the price is shared: retailer (shop) 50%, brand 25%, factory owner 12%, materials (cotton, fabric) 9%, transport and taxes 3%, factory worker’s wages 1%. Suggest why the data should be used with caution.
items.answer: It is an estimate for one product; shares vary between brands, countries and years; the study’s method and source are not given.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Evaluate the view that transnational companies bring more benefits than problems to lower-income countries.
items.answer: Agree: They create jobs and training, bring investment and technology, and earn export income (e.g. Bangladesh’s garment exports). Disagree: Wages can be very low and conditions dangerous (Rana Plaza 2013). Profits are sent abroad and TNCs may move if costs rise. Pollution and loss of local firms. Judgement: TNCs can bring important benefits, but these depend on host-country regulation, workers’ rights and consumer pressure.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: Name the term that matches this definition: “improvement in people’s standard of living and quality of life, including wealth, health and education”.
items.answer: Development
items.markingKey: Development: improvement in people’s standard of living and quality of life, including wealth, health and education. [1]

items.stem: Explain why GDP per capita alone is not a good measure of development.
items.answer: It is an average that hides inequality within a country; it does not measure health, education, freedom or environmental quality; informal economic activity is not counted.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each point up to [3]

items.stem: Explain why the HDI is a better measure of development than GDP per capita.
items.answer: It combines economic (income) and social measures (life expectancy and education), so it gives a broader picture of people’s quality of life.
items.markingKey: 1 mark combines measures; 1 mark broader picture [2]

items.stem: “The Sustainable Development Goals are too ambitious to be achieved by 2030.” Discuss this view, explaining points for and against, and reach a supported conclusion. You may wish to consider: COVID-19 and conflict; funding.
items.answer: Agree: UN reports show many targets are off track; COVID-19, conflict and climate change have reversed progress on poverty and hunger. Disagree: Goals set direction and focus funding; some targets (e.g. electricity access, child mortality) have improved significantly. Ambitious goals inspire action by governments, businesses and citizens. Judgement: Many goals will probably not be fully met by 2030, but they remain valuable as a shared plan for action.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: Explain what is meant by the three pillars of sustainable development, with an example of each.
items.answer: Economic (decent jobs and growth, e.g. SDG 8), social (health, education and equality, e.g. SDGs 3, 4, 5) and environmental (protecting climate, land and oceans, e.g. SDGs 13-15); sustainable development balances all three.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each pillar with example [3]

items.stem: Explain how improvements in transport have encouraged globalisation.
items.answer: Container ships, larger aircraft and better ports have made moving goods and people faster and cheaper, so companies can buy and sell around the world and tourism and migration have grown.
items.markingKey: 1 mark example; 1 mark faster/cheaper; 1 mark effect on trade/people [3]

items.stem: “Improvements in technology have been the main cause of globalisation.” Discuss this view, explaining points for and against, and reach a supported conclusion. You may wish to consider: TNCs; trade agreements.
items.answer: Agree: Containerisation, jet aircraft and the internet have made trade and communication fast and cheap. Disagree: Political decisions – GATT (1947), the WTO (1995), free-trade agreements and China opening its economy – removed barriers. Transnational companies seeking profit drove the spread of production. Judgement: Technology made globalisation possible, but political and economic decisions explain its speed and direction.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: “Consumers are mainly responsible for improving conditions in global supply chains.” How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer. You may wish to consider: TNCs; governments; consumers.
items.answer: Agree: Consumer choices and campaigns pushed brands to sign the Bangladesh Accord after Rana Plaza. Disagree: Governments set and enforce labour laws. TNCs control supply chains and prices. Trade unions and NGOs press for change; many consumers cannot afford ethical products. Judgement: Consumers have influence, but governments and companies hold the greatest responsibility.

options: The difference in standards of living between the richest and poorest countries.
The number of babies who die before their first birthday per 1000 live births.
A raw material or crop, such as cocoa, coffee or copper, sold without being processed.
Improvement in people’s standard of living and quality of life, including wealth, health and education.
items.answer: Improvement in people’s standard of living and quality of life, including wealth, health and education.
items.markingKey: Development: improvement in people’s standard of living and quality of life, including wealth, health and education. [1]

items.stem: Explain how Fairtrade can benefit farming communities, using an example.
items.answer: The minimum price protects farmers when world prices fall; the premium is spent democratically on projects – e.g. Kenyan Fairtrade flower farms have funded schools, clinics and clean water.

items.stem: A farmers’ cooperative sells 100 000 kg of Fairtrade coffee. The world market price is US$2.2 per kg. The Fairtrade minimum price is US$2.4 per kg and the Fairtrade premium is US$0.2 per kg. (a) Calculate the income from selling at the world market price. (b) Calculate the total extra income from Fairtrade compared with the world price.
Evaluate the view that fair trade is the best way to reduce inequality between countries. You may wish to consider: trade rules; scale of fair trade; investment and aid.
items.answer: Agree: Guaranteed minimum prices and premiums improve farmers’ incomes, schools and health care (e.g. Kenyan flower farms). Disagree: Fairtrade is a small share of world trade. Processing products locally, investment, education, debt relief and fairer trade rules may have bigger effects. Good governance and reducing conflict matter. Judgement: Fair trade helps specific communities but cannot on its own close the development gap.

items.stem: Explain why the SDGs are linked to each other.
items.answer: Progress on one helps others: e.g. clean water (SDG 6) improves health (SDG 3) and lets girls attend school instead of collecting water (SDGs 4 and 5); climate action (SDG 13) protects food production (SDG 2).
items.markingKey: 1 mark link; 1 mark example [2]

items.stem: “Governments, not individuals, should take the lead in achieving the SDGs.” Discuss this view, explaining points for and against, and reach a supported conclusion.
items.answer: Agree: Governments control laws, budgets and international agreements, and can act at large scale. Disagree: Businesses, NGOs, communities and individuals also make a difference, e.g. reducing waste, campaigning, volunteering. Many local projects are led by communities. Individual pressure pushes governments to act. Judgement: Governments must lead, but the goals need action at every level.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: Name the term that matches this definition: “goods and services bought from other countries”.
items.answer: Imports
items.markingKey: Imports: goods and services bought from other countries. [1]

items.stem: Explain how the internet and mobile phones have speeded up globalisation.
items.answer: Instant, cheap communication lets companies manage factories and offices worldwide, trade online and outsource services such as call centres; ideas, news and culture spread instantly.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each point up to [3]

items.stem: Country T exported goods and services worth US$200 billion and imported goods and services worth US$220 billion in one year. Its GDP was US$400 billion. Suggest two ways the country could increase its exports.
items.answer: Join trade agreements to reduce tariffs; improve ports and transport; attract foreign companies; develop higher-value manufacturing or services.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: “Improvements in technology have been the main cause of globalisation.” Discuss this view, explaining points for and against, and reach a supported conclusion. You may wish to consider: communication; trade agreements; TNCs.
items.answer: Agree: Containerisation, jet aircraft and the internet have made trade and communication fast and cheap. Disagree: Political decisions – GATT (1947), the WTO (1995), free-trade agreements and China opening its economy – removed barriers. Transnational companies seeking profit drove the spread of production. Judgement: Technology made globalisation possible, but political and economic decisions explain its speed and direction.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: Name the term that matches this definition: “when a company pays another company, often in another country, to carry out part of its work”.
items.answer: Outsourcing
items.markingKey: Outsourcing: when a company pays another company, often in another country, to carry out part of its work. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “All TNCs have their headquarters in Europe or North America.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Many large TNCs are based in Asia, e.g. Toyota (Japan), Samsung (South Korea), Tata (India) and Huawei (China).
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate supporting explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain why long global supply chains can be risky.
items.answer: A problem at one point – a pandemic, disaster, war or blocked canal – can stop production elsewhere, as in COVID-19 (2020) and the Suez blockage (2021); just-in-time systems have few spare stocks.
items.markingKey: 1 mark one failure affects whole chain; 1 mark example [2]

items.stem: A study of a T-shirt sold for US$25 in Europe estimated how the price is shared: retailer (shop) 50%, brand 25%, factory owner 12%, materials (cotton, fabric) 9%, transport and taxes 3%, factory worker’s wages 1%. If the worker’s share doubled, calculate the new price assuming every other share stays the same in money terms.

A study of a T-shirt sold for US$30 in Europe estimated how the price is shared: retailer (shop) 55%, brand 20%, factory owner 10%, materials (cotton, fabric) 11%, transport and taxes 3%, factory worker’s wages 1%. (a) Calculate how much the retailer receives. (b) Suggest why the data should be used with caution.
items.answer: (a) US$16.5 (b) It is an estimate for one product; shares vary between brands, countries and years; the study’s method and source are not given.

items.stem: Evaluate the view that transnational companies bring more benefits than problems to lower-income countries. You may wish to consider: safety; jobs and wages; regulation.
items.answer: Agree: They create jobs and training, bring investment and technology, and earn export income (e.g. Bangladesh’s garment exports). Disagree: Wages can be very low and conditions dangerous (Rana Plaza 2013). Profits are sent abroad and TNCs may move if costs rise. Pollution and loss of local firms. Judgement: TNCs can bring important benefits, but these depend on host-country regulation, workers’ rights and consumer pressure.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: What is meant by the term “GDP per capita”?
options: Extra money paid to Fairtrade producer groups to spend on community projects such as schools and clean water.
The percentage of adults who can read and write.
A trading system that guarantees producers in poorer countries a minimum price and a premium to invest in their communities.
The total value of goods and services produced by a country in a year divided by its population.
items.answer: The total value of goods and services produced by a country in a year divided by its population.
items.markingKey: GDP per capita: the total value of goods and services produced by a country in a year divided by its population. [1]

items.stem: A classmate claims: “Kenyan roses flown to Europe always have a bigger carbon footprint than roses grown in Europe.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Some studies found roses from heated Dutch greenhouses produced more emissions than Kenyan roses grown in natural sunlight, even including the flight.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate supporting explanation [2]

items.stem: Development indicators (approximate, early 2020s) – HDI, life expectancy (years), infant mortality (per 1000 live births), adult literacy (%): Kenya 0.601, 63, 31, 83; Brazil 0.76, 76, 13, 94; Nepal 0.601, 70, 22, 71. Suggest one other indicator that would help compare these countries, and explain why.
items.answer: GNI per capita (wealth), percentage with access to clean water, doctors per 1000 people, or gender inequality – each adds a different aspect of quality of life.
items.markingKey: 1 mark indicator; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: A farmers’ cooperative sells 20 000 kg of Fairtrade coffee. The world market price is US$2.2 per kg. The Fairtrade minimum price is US$2.4 per kg and the Fairtrade premium is US$0.2 per kg. (a) Calculate the income from selling at the Fairtrade minimum price. (b) Calculate the total Fairtrade premium paid to the cooperative.
items.markingKey: (a) 20000 × 2.4 (minimum price applies because the world price is lower) [1] (b) 20000 × 0.2 [1]

items.stem: Development indicators (approximate, early 2020s) – HDI, life expectancy (years), infant mortality (per 1000 live births), adult literacy (%): Niger 0.394, 62, 60, 38; Nepal 0.601, 70, 22, 71; Kenya 0.601, 63, 31, 83. (a) Suggest one other indicator that would help compare these countries, and explain why. (b) Calculate how many times higher the infant mortality rate is in Niger than in Nepal.
items.answer: (a) GNI per capita (wealth), percentage with access to clean water, doctors per 1000 people, or gender inequality – each adds a different aspect of quality of life. (b) 2.7 times
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark indicator; 1 mark reason [2] (b) 60 ÷ 22 [1]

items.stem: “The Human Development Index is the best way to measure development.” Discuss this view, explaining points for and against, and reach a supported conclusion. You may wish to consider: education; life expectancy; inequality.
items.answer: Agree: It combines health, education and income, giving a broad picture. Disagree: It ignores inequality, freedom, gender and the environment; national averages hide regional differences. Other measures (e.g. the Multidimensional Poverty Index, Gender Inequality Index) add detail. Judgement: The HDI is a good single measure, but development is best measured with several indicators.

items.stem: A student writes: “The SDGs only apply to low-income countries.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. They are universal and apply to every country, including high-income countries.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate supporting explanation [2]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Clean water and sanitation is one of the 17 SDGs.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. It is SDG 6.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate supporting explanation [2]

items.stem: In a development project, women farmers in Bangladesh receive training and small loans to grow and sell vegetables. Explain why community involvement is important for the project to be sustainable.
items.answer: Local people understand their needs, will maintain and repair the project, and feel ownership, so it continues after outside funding ends.
items.markingKey: 1 mark ownership/maintenance; 1 mark long-term [2]

items.stem: “The Sustainable Development Goals are too ambitious to be achieved by 2030.” Discuss this view, explaining points for and against, and reach a supported conclusion. You may wish to consider: value of targets; progress so far; funding.
items.answer: Agree: UN reports show many targets are off track; COVID-19, conflict and climate change have reversed progress on poverty and hunger. Disagree: Goals set direction and focus funding; some targets (e.g. electricity access, child mortality) have improved significantly. Ambitious goals inspire action by governments, businesses and citizens. Judgement: Many goals will probably not be fully met by 2030, but they remain valuable as a shared plan for action.
